issue_context.title: pd.ExcelFile closes stream on destruction in pandas 1.0.0
issue_context.body:
#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example if possible

```python3

import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)
a = open('some_file.xlsx', 'rb')
x = pd.ExcelFile(a)
del x
print(a.read())
```


#### Problem description

Above script behaves in different way in pandas 0.25.3 and 1.0.0:

```bash
$ python3 t1.py
0.25.3
b''
$ sudo pip3 install pandas --upgrade --quiet
$ python3 t1.py
1.0.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "t1.py", line 6, in <module>
    print(a.read())
ValueError: read of closed file
```

It seems that stream is closed when ExcelFile is destroyed - and I don't see why.

#### Expected Output

I'd expect either notice in release notes, or the same output in 0.25.3 and 1.0.0.

comments:
Possibly related to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/30096 since that added a `__del__` (cc @jbrockmendel), although I would assume that the `ExcelFile.close()` should not necessarily close the file handle (in which case it is not related to that PR).

@johny-b if you do `x.close()` instead of `del x`, is the file stream also closed?
I don’t think this is a bug. del simply decrements a reference count but makes no guarantees around when the GC will actually destroy the object.

in read_csv where we track if an open stream is given (as opposed to a file), then can close *only* things that we opened. this might take a bit of work to fix though.

if someone wants to do this for 1.0.1 great, but won't consider this a blocker.

Yes, the "bug" (or missing feature, how you want to call it) is that that `close()` should only close the file handle if it was opened by pandas itself. 
The fact that now `__del__` closes the file handle is only because `__del__` now calls `close()`, which was a corect fix, but it surfaced the close issue.

It seems that the changes for #3441 (PR #4933) introduced this statement (in 2013). The changes have been carried forward to this day, but seem to be obsolete or already covered by other code that closes file handles.

review_comments: Is there a way to construct this test without the `del` call? This test might not be doing anything, since `del` doesn't really mean `__del__` gets called

`__del__` will get called in practice when the last reference is `del`eted. This is needed to trigger the erroneous behavior.
This is literally the code in the OP's issue. (except I replaced `ExcelFile` with `read_excel`, it seems)
Can you revert this? Not totally equivalent

It is indeed not equivalent, but that is on purpose. The test is faulty. First you open a file and fail to close it, then you check for a file leak. This demonstrates in fact the issue we are having. Ownership of the file handle should be managed at the level it is created, unless you explicitly transfer ownership of the file handle to `ExcelFile`, but IMHO that is not what you would expect (and the reason for the ticket)

Yea I think this test strays a little bit from the OP, where a straight ExcelFile object is closing the handle. In this case the context manager is closing it, which maybe is OK. I can't speak to original history of this.

So @roberthdevries can you maybe summarize what you are proposing? Something like:

 1. ExcelFile Context Manager + path: should manage open/close lifecycle
 2. ExcelFile Context Manager + handle: should not manage open/close lifecycle
 3. ExcelFile + path: should manage open, not close
 4. ExcelFile + handle: should not manage open/close lifecycle

? 

I think point 2 above is a little ambiguous; if there's a precedent for it elsewhere would be interested

I think the basic philosophy should be that a resource should be released at the same level where it was created. This is one of the main use cases of context managers.
So whenever a resource is released at **another** level, you violate this rule. (hence this ticket)
The original `ExcelFile` code closed a file it got from the outside, and this specific test relied on this (erroneous IMHO) behavior.
So a nested context manager should work as expected, in the sense that the outside context manager releases the outer resource and the inner context manager releases the inner resource.

So:
```python
with open("foo.xlsx") as f:
    with ExcelFile(f) as xlsx:
        # do stuff
```
In this specific example the `ExcelFile` context manager should **not** close `f`, as that would be the responsibility of the `open` context manager.

In this example:
```python
f = open("foo.xlsx")
with ExcelFile(f) as xlsx:
    # do stuff
```
We have a file leak caused by the programmer forgetting to close the file handle. This is a programmer error, and IMHO not something that needs to be fixed.
However, whenever `f` goes out of scope, the `__del__` method will be called which will probably close the file anyway.

For use cases where `ExcelFile` is used in combination with path names the context manager case implies closing the file.
In this case:
```python
xlsx = ExcelFile(filename)
```
I would propose to have a `__del__` method which will close the file and the other `ExcelFile` resources.

So I agree with you on case 1 and 4.
I also agree with case 2, there is no ambiguity for me. The `ExcelFile` context manager only should manage its own resources, not the file resource.
For case 3 there should be a nuance in the sense that the `__del__` method should close the resource.
For case 4, the `ExcelFile` should not touch the open/close lifecyle of the file handle, but the `ExcelFile` resource itself should be closed again in the `__del__` method.

Thanks for the insights. So agree with what you are saying but not sure that is clearly expressed in the implementation. Shouldn't we alternately just within the ExcelFile construct or `__enter__` keep track of whether or not the resource lifecycle is owned or borrowed? As is I don't think that's ever very clear

> Shouldn't we alternately just within the ExcelFile constructor

That seems most sensible to me. Do we have a standard method for checking if something is a file-like object vs. a path?
It ends up not being an issue here since ExcelFile doesn't open any files, just the engine.
Would it make sense to make this an abstract method, and make child classes be explicit on how the close is performed (including when no close is performed)?
In an earlier version of this PR, this was an abstract method, but the powers that be preferred this.
We can't make a new abstract method in a bugfix release. Any child not implementing it would fail when the class is instantiated.
Is this intentionally removed? Wondering if there is any engine that needs this...
